design-patterns/design-patterns.html.description:
Design patterns in software engineering are reusable, proven solutions to common, recurring problems in software design.There are 3 types of design patterns:
Creational: Focus on Mechanisms for creating objects
Structural: Deals with how to structure classes
Behavioral: Deals with behavior of classes with each other.

design-principles/lod.html.title: LOD
design-principles/lod.html.description:
Law of Demeter : Only talk to your immediate friends.The rule is straightforward. A method M on an object O should only call methods on:
Itself (the object O)
Its own fields (objects that O holds as instance variables like DI)
Its method parameters (objects passed into M)
Objects it creates (objects instantiated within M)
 don't reach through one object to get to another.If you inject IMyService into your class:
Allowed: _myService.DoWork() (Talking to a direct friend).
Violation: _myService.Configuration.DatabaseSettings.ConnectionString

design-principles/srp.html.title: SRP
design-principles/srp.html.description: #solid_princliples "A class should have one, and only one reason to change." "A class should have only one stakeholder". "A module should do one job." The change can be requested by only one stakeholder. The God Class A class that tries to do everything. Things that try to do everything do nothing well. Focus on cohesion, not fragmentation. Group logic that changes together or belongs to the same business concern.

design-principles/yagni.html.description: You ain't gonna need it!Don't implement stuff just because you foresee a requirement, only do it when you actually need it.

4-pillars-of-oops.html.title: 4 Pillars of OOPs
4-pillars-of-oops.html.description:
Class RelationshipsIn this type of relationship, two objects use or know about each other. They can exist independently of each other.Example: A student has a teacher, both can exist independently of each other.class PaymentGateway { public: void processPayment(double value){ std::cout<< std::format("Processing payment for value: {}", value); } }; // Order has-a payment gateway class Order { private: std::string orderId_; public: PaymentGateway* gateway; Order(PaymentGateway* gateway) : gateway(gateway) {}; void checkout(double value){ this->gateway->processPayment(value); } }; The above example is for unidirectional association, there also can be bidirectional association (both classes are aware of each other).class Developer { private: Team* team; public: void setTeam(Team* team) { this->team = team; } }; class Team { private: vector<Developer*> developers; public: void addDeveloper(Developer* dev) { developers.push_back(dev); dev->setTeam(this); } }; There is 1-1, 1-many, many-1, many-many associations possible.
This is subset of Association , which implies a stronger whole-part relationship. The parts can exist without the whole and the parts can be shuffled/shared.For example: A team contains football players, players can exist independently as well. Or professors in department.This is tight coupling and the two entities are connected through a container-contained hierarchy.This is the strongest form of has-a relationship. Where toe whole owns the parts and controls their lifecycles. The part cannot exist without the whole.Example: Roads and speed breakers, House and Rooms, Car and its components.class SpeedBreaker { public: SpeedBreaker() { std::cout << " [Part] Speed breaker created.\n"; } ~SpeedBreaker() { std::cout << " [Part] Speed breaker destroyed.\n"; } }; class Road { private: std::vector<SpeedBreaker> breakers; public: Road(int count) { std::cout << "[Whole] Building Road...\n"; breakers.resize(count); } }; A dependency exists when one class relies on another to do something, but does so without retaining a permanent reference to it.This can be done via the following ways: Accept/Return another class in/from a method Instantiate a class in a method. Depend on an interface instead of concrete types. Example: A chef and a knife, chef's cut method can cut things with the knife but then he doesn't need to keep the knife with him forever.// Accept/Return another class in/from a method class EventPublisher {}; class EventPublisherFactory { public: EventPublisher createEventPublisher(const std::string &topic_name) { return EventPublisher(); }; }; class Canvas { public: void drawSprite(std::string name, int x, int y) { std::cout << "Drawing " << name << " at (" << x << "," << y << ")\n"; } }; class Player { private: std::string name = "Hero"; int x = 10, y = 20; public: void render(Canvas& currentScreen) { // Does not make sense to store hard reference to canvas since it might be recreated in the next scene currentScreen.drawSprite(name, x, y); } }; // Instantiate class in a method class JsonFormatter { public: std::string format(const std::string &message){ return "{\"message\":\"" + message + "\"}"; } }; void printAsJson(const std::string &message){ JsonFormatter formatter; std::cout << formatter.format(message); } When dependencies are provided from outside, it is known as dependency injection. You can let the objects create the objects of dependencies but that introduces tight coupling and reduces reusability.This is usually done through a constructor.class StorageService { private: BlobContainerClient* blobContainerClient; public: StorageService(BlobContainerClient &containerClient) : blobContainerClient(containerClient) {} }

info_attractionForce.description: How much should linked nodes attract each other? This will make the graph appear more clustered.

info_linkLength.description: How long should the links between nodes be? The shorter the links the more connected nodes will cluster together.

info_repulsionForce.description: How much should nodes repel each other? This will make disconnected parts more spread out.

info_centralForce.description: How much should nodes be attracted to the center? This will make the graph appear more dense and circular.

info_edgePruning.description: Edges with a length above this threshold will not be rendered, however they will still contribute to the simulation. This can help large tangled graphs look more organised. Hovering over a node will still display these links.

info_minNodeRadius.description: How small should the smallest nodes be? The smaller a node is the less it will attract other nodes.

info_maxNodeRadius.description: How large should the largest nodes be? Nodes are sized by how many links they have. The larger a node is the more it will attract other nodes. This can be used to create a good grouping around the most important nodes.
